heard: Why can’t you just start paying again?
where: servicer calls · VA higher-level-review responses · hearing testimony · comment sections
record_says: Being able to resume payments is the partial-claim test. An ongoing hardship is not.
authority: 38 U.S.C. § 3737(a), three conditions: VA-guaranteed loan · primary residence · in default or at imminent risk of default. The same standard applied to the COVID-era program: 38 CFR § 36.4803(d) required that "the veteran indicates that the veteran can resume making scheduled monthly payments, on time and in full." Ability to resume the payment, not resolution of the hardship, in both programs, five years apart. MERGED FROM LIVE: the resolution-of-hardship condition belongs to the loan-modification rule, 38 C.F.R. § 36.4315(a)(2), not to the partial-claim rule.
say_back: "The partial claim exists for borrowers who can resume the regular payment but cannot cure the arrears, that’s the statutory test. I can resume the regular monthly payment. I’m asking for the arrears to be handled under the partial claim." If you were told this, ask in writing which rule’s eligibility criteria were applied, and cite § 36.4803(d).
if_again: Request the denial in writing with the specific eligibility criterion cited. File CFPB attaching the written denial.
notes: The two sources argue the same point from different regulations. Both authorities kept: the cross-program consistency argument and the wrong-rule argument are separately useful.

heard: "You don’t qualify, you’re already in foreclosure."
where: servicer calls · loss-mitigation denials
record_says: The statute makes loans in default eligible. The no-foreclosure bar is agency-added, not statutory.
authority: § 3737(a)(3) makes loans "in default or at imminent risk of default" eligible. The "no pending/active foreclosure" bar is M26-4 Ch. 22 § 22.02 a.5 (FINAL, June 1 2026), not in the statute.
say_back: "The statute makes loans in default eligible, that’s the whole point of the program. The bar you’re citing is in VA’s handbook, not the law. Please cite the statutory provision that disqualifies me."
if_again: Put "cite the statutory provision" in writing to VA and to your congressional office. An unanswered request for a citation is itself a finding.
notes: One of the seven VA-added gates. CORRECTED 2026-08-28 from “six” on Leann’s word: /record/policy/ states “Seven of the ten eligibility rules … appear nowhere in the law Congress passed” and names section 22.02, and the 2026-08-10 MASTER brief says seven. heard: "You had a loan modification recently, so you’re locked out."
where: servicer loss-mitigation reviews
record_says: The 24-month modification lockout was written by the agency, not by Congress.
authority: M26-4 Ch. 22 § 22.02 a.7 (FINAL, June 1 2026), not in § 3737. Verified: this criterion appears in the final chapter and not in the February 2026 draft. The draft instead required six payments since the most recent modification. The final replaced that with a flat 24-month lockout.
say_back: "That restriction isn’t in the statute. If a prior modification was itself unaffordable or improperly offered, please explain how it can now disqualify me from the remedy Congress created."
if_again: Note the serial-modification trap in the CFPB complaint: a bad modification creating a 24-month lockout from the statutory remedy.
notes: Pairs with PR-19, this is one of the two criteria added after the comment window closed.

heard: "You filed bankruptcy, so you’re not eligible."
where: servicer loss-mitigation reviews
record_says: Congress wrote no bankruptcy bar. The agency did.
authority: M26-4 Ch. 22 § 22.02 a.4 (FINAL, June 1 2026), not in § 3737. Dismissed Ch. 7, dismissed or discharged Ch. 13, and discharged Ch. 7 with reaffirmation are carved out.
say_back: "Active bankruptcy isn’t a statutory disqualifier. If my case is dismissed or discharged, the handbook’s own carve-outs apply. Please state which subsection you’re relying on."
if_again: This is the catch-22: bankruptcy is often the only emergency stay against eviction, and using it forecloses the loss-mitigation remedy. Document it for oversight.

heard: "The home isn’t in your name anymore."
where: post-foreclosure · successor-in-interest situations · after divorce or a death

say_back: "The statute refers to the borrower. The owner-of-record condition comes from VA’s handbook. Please identify the statutory basis."
if_again: This is a primary mechanism excluding already-foreclosed families. Raise it as an oversight item, not a servicer dispute, the servicer can’t waive it.

heard: "You were offered help and you turned it down." / "They were offered help and refused it."

In reported cohort cases the "assistance" offered was a modification that raised the interest rate several points, on fixed incomes, raising the payment by half or more.
say_back: "I didn’t decline assistance. I declined one offer that wasn’t affordable. Please send the written evaluation notice for every option I was evaluated for, and the reason each was denied." Get every offer’s rate, payment, and denial reasons in writing; compare the new rate to your existing rate plus one point.

heard: "If it was really illegal, why don’t they just sue?"
where: comment sections · staffer conversations · family self-blame
record_says: The clock is short, the remedy is capped, the fee recovery is thin, and a foreclosed former owner is a category most free legal aid does not cover.
authority: The federal deadlines are the same in every state. RESPA servicing claims under 12 U.S.C. 2605 carry three years, set by 12 U.S.C. 2614, running "from the date of the occurrence of the violation." The statute text contains no discovery rule, so the clock starts when the conduct happened, not when you found out. Most Truth in Lending damages claims carry one year under 15 U.S.C. 1640(e), with three years for claims under 15 U.S.C. 1639, 1639b or 1639c. Fair Credit Reporting claims under 15 U.S.C. 1681p carry the EARLIER of two years after you discover the violation or five years after it occurs; earlier, not later. State deadlines vary and Washington is a worked example only. The Washington Consumer Protection Act carries four years under RCW 19.86.120. Washington post-sale claims are governed by RCW 61.24.127(2)(a), which requires a claim be brought "within two years from the date of the foreclosure sale or within the applicable statute of limitations for such claim, whichever expires earlier." A longer federal period does not extend it. What a court may award is also limited: RCW 61.24.127(2) allows money only, says the claim "may not affect in any way the validity or finality of the foreclosure sale," prohibits recording a lis pendens, and limits relief to actual damages unless a Consumer Protection Act claim rides along, in which case treble damages and a reasonable attorney's fee become available under RCW 19.86.090, which caps the increased award for a RCW 19.86.020 violation at twenty-five thousand dollars. Statutory damages are small: RESPA gives actual damages plus, only for a pattern or practice, an amount "not to exceed $2,000" under 12 U.S.C. 2605(f)(1), and TILA statutory damages on a closed-end mortgage are "not less than $400 or greater than $4,000" under 15 U.S.C. 1640(a)(2)(A)(iv). Two things here are not statutes and matter as much. Legal aid is organised around a category a foreclosed former owner falls outside of: in August 2026 Washington's statewide civil legal aid provider declined a case in this cohort because it was a foreclosure eviction rather than a standard unlawful detainer. The obstacle was category, not capacity. And the private bar is thin for a documented reason: an attorney told the family that lawyers left the consumer foreclosure defence speciality after the 2007 to 2008 housing crash and did not come back, and that state-by-state licensing narrows the pool further for a cohort spread across many states.
receipt: CAPTURE: 12 U.S.C. 2614; 15 U.S.C. 1640(e); 15 U.S.C. 1681p; 12 U.S.C. 2605(f)(1); 15 U.S.C. 1640(a)(2)(A)(iv); RCW 19.86.120; RCW 19.86.090; RCW 61.24.127(2) captured as a whole subsection. Plus a dated, de-identified record of the legal-aid declination.
say_back: "I am a former owner after a foreclosure sale, not a tenant, so the eviction programs in my area may not cover me. Before anything else I need to know which deadlines are already running. Under 12 U.S.C. 2614 a RESPA servicing claim is three years from the date the violation happened, not from when I found out. Under 15 U.S.C. 1640(e) most Truth in Lending damages claims are one year. My state may put a separate and shorter deadline on anything raised after the sale. Can you tell me which of my dates have already passed and which have not?"
if_again: This belongs in state legislative outreach and access-to-justice funding, not in a servicer dispute. A servicer cannot lengthen a statutory deadline and has no reason to try.
status: HOLD, research complete, needs receipt captures before publishing
notes: Pairs with PR-26; PR-14 is why suing is hard, PR-26 is why a referral does not close the gap. heard: "You already got COVID help, so you can’t get this."
where: servicer loss-mitigation reviews · VA responses · anywhere a family took COVID-era assistance

M26-4 Ch. 22 § 22.02 a.10 (FINAL, June 1 2026) extends the disqualification to a COVID-19 Veterans Assistance Partial Claim Payment under 38 C.F.R. part 36 subpart F, and to a COVID-19 Refund Modification. Neither is a § 3737 partial claim.

heard: "Homeowners have more legal protection than renters."
where: comment sections · legal-aid intake · anywhere post-foreclosure occupancy comes up
record_says: After a foreclosure sale, the former owner usually has less protection than a tenant in the same building.
authority: In Washington a tenant in a foreclosed property gets sixty days' written notice to vacate under RCW 61.24.146, and that section says in terms that it does not apply if the borrower or grantor remains on the property. RCW 61.24.060(1) gives the purchaser possession on the twentieth day as against the borrower and grantor and occupants who are not tenants. The appointed-counsel provision, RCW 59.18.640(1), is written for an indigent TENANT in unlawful detainer proceedings under chapters 59.18, 59.12 and 59.20, and it is expressly SUBJECT TO THE AVAILABILITY OF AMOUNTS APPROPRIATED FOR THIS SPECIFIC PURPOSE. So the notice protection excludes the former owner on the face of the statute, and the counsel provision is written for tenants and is funding-contingent even for them. Wyoming has a three-month statutory redemption with the right to remain during it; Washington has none.
say_back: "In Washington a tenant in a foreclosed property gets sixty days' written notice, and that section says it does not apply if the borrower or grantor stays on the property. The purchaser gets possession on the twentieth day. The appointed-counsel statute is written for an indigent tenant and is subject to available appropriations. I am the former owner, so I have twenty days and I should not count on counsel."
if_again: This is a state-law finding. It belongs in state legislative outreach, not in a servicer dispute.

heard: "VA cannot impose a foreclosure moratorium."
where: agency testimony · constituent-services replies · committee correspondence
record_says: VA pressed for one twice, in November 2023 and again in May 2024, and published its reasons in the circulars both times.
authority: VBA Circular 26-23-25 (November 30, 2023) section 3 strongly encouraged a foreclosure moratorium on all VA-guaranteed loans through May 31, 2024, excepting vacant or abandoned properties. VBA Circular 26-24-12 (May 29, 2024) section 3 extended relief as a TARGETED moratorium through December 31, 2024. As issued it named four exceptions: vacant or abandoned; borrower documented as not wanting retention or to avoid foreclosure; no payment for at least 210 days with no response to outreach; all retention options including VASP evaluated and none workable. Change 1, issued June 21, 2024, deleted the 210-day exception (S197), so for most of the moratorium there were three, not four. The base circular was never reissued, so the PDF VA still serves at that address prints the deleted paragraph. Neither circular imposes a moratorium. Both encourage one, and both cite 38 U.S.C. 3704(d) and 38 C.F.R. 36.4336, the power to audit a servicer and bar it from the program.
say_back: "VA has done this twice. Circular 26-23-25, November 30, 2023, strongly encouraged a moratorium on all VA-guaranteed loans through May 31, 2024. Circular 26-24-12, May 29, 2024, extended it as a targeted moratorium through December 31, 2024. Both gave the reason in the text: to buy servicers time to stand up the program. What has VA done for the November 28, 2026 deadline?"

group: C. Authority and the agency’s own numbers
heard: "Veterans already get plenty of programs and benefits."
where: comment sections · congressional replies · agency testimony · anywhere the ask is framed as special treatment
record_says: Veterans got worse options than everyone else, not better ones. That is the whole finding.
authority: FHA, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac all retained permanent partial-claim programs. VA let its COVID-era partial claim lapse in 2022, built VASP as the replacement, and cancelled VASP in May 2025 with nothing operational behind it, the only federal mortgage system to remove the safety net twice. Separately, the Homeowner Assistance Fund, the one program available to everyone else, disqualified veteran households because VA disability compensation was counted as income.
say_back: "Every other federal mortgage system kept its safety net. The VA is the only one that removed it, twice. And the fund everyone else could use counted a veteran’s disability compensation as income, so it did not reach us. This is not a request for more than other people get. It is a request for the same thing."
if_again: Ask which comparable federal mortgage program lacks a partial claim. There is not one.

group: C. Authority and the agency’s own numbers

record_says: The default is not in the loans people bought. It is in the loans that were rewritten for them. Veterans who bought a home in the last two years are defaulting BELOW the average for the whole VA book.
authority: Ginnie Mae MBS loan level disclosure, llmon2_202606, complete pooled VA book, 3,821,399 loans, June 2026. Never-modified loans are 90+ days delinquent at 1.32 to 1.90 percent. Modified loans, 12.52 to 16.88 percent. Purchases with a first payment on or after July 2024 default at 1.53 percent against a 2.0 percent book average.

heard: "They were offered a loan modification, so they were helped." / "A modification is a home retention option." / "The servicer did offer them something."
where: servicer responses · VA higher-level-review letters · congressional replies · agency testimony
record_says: A modification is only help if the payment goes down. Across the whole VA book, a modified loan carrying a 7 to 8 percent note is 90 or more days delinquent at 36.3 percent. A modified loan under 3 percent is at 5.67 percent. Same program, same borrowers, same crisis. The remedy failed as a function of how it was written.
authority: Ginnie Mae MBS loan level disclosure, llmon2_202606, complete pooled VA book, 3,821,399 loans, June 2026, current note rate field on every loan, zero unusable values. Modified VA loans, 90+ days delinquent by current note rate: under 3 percent 5.67; 3 to 4 percent 6.69; 4 to 5 percent 8.59; 5 to 6 percent 15.68; 6 to 7 percent 18.26; 7 to 8 percent 36.30. Modifications with a first payment on or after July 2024 carrying a 7 to 8 percent note: 11,944 loans, 4,584 seriously delinquent, 38.38 percent. At the identical note rate a modified loan defaults 4 to 7 times a never-modified one (7 to 8 percent band: 36.30 against 9.37). A 40-year term appears nowhere in the VA book except among modifications: 34,201 loans, 23.91 percent seriously delinquent, against 1.67 percent for a never-modified loan on a normal term.
receipt: CAPTURE: the note-rate field on the layout page; the gradient table published as a figure with rate_by_purpose_out.csv alongside
say_back: "A modification is help only if the payment goes down. Across the whole VA book, a modified loan at seven to eight percent is ninety days delinquent at thirty-six percent. A modified loan under three percent, three years into the same crisis, is at five point seven. The modifications that kept the payment down worked. The ones that raised it did not. That is not a story about borrowers. It is a story about what they were handed."
if_again: "Compare it to a veteran who simply bought at seven percent. That borrower defaults at nine percent. A veteran modified into seven percent defaults at thirty-six. Four times worse at the same rate. Raising a distressed household’s payment is not a remedy for distress."

heard: “VASP was a bailout for lenders.”
where: committee press releases · agency testimony · congressional replies
record_says: The same statement that said it named the replacement: a partial claim so veterans could stay in their homes. Congress passed that in July 2025. It still is not running.
authority: Joint statement of Chairman Mike Bost and Rep. Derrick Van Orden, House Committee on Veterans' Affairs, April 3 2025. Verbatim: “The Biden-Harris administration wrongfully jeopardized the future of this benefit by allowing billions of dollars to be used towards bailouts for lenders by creating the VASP program.” The same statement, four sentences later: “This action underscores House Republicans' intent to establish a partial claims program at VA to ensure veterans' can stay in their homes if they're in financial hardship while still protecting the American taxpayer.” It also carries the committee's own fiscal case: “Instead of reinstituting the partial claim program for an average loan delinquency of $22,500, VA chose to purchase these loans through the VASP program at an average of $292,000,” a figure the statement says has since risen to $320,000. H.R. 1815 passed the House on May 19 2025 under suspension of the rules, which requires a two-thirds majority, by voice vote, and passed the Senate without amendment by voice vote on July 15 2025. It was signed July 30 2025. Neither chamber held a roll-call vote, so no individual vote tally or recorded opposition exists. VA called the Partial Claim Program live on June 15 2026 and set full servicer implementation at no later than November 28 2026.
say_back: “That is from the April 3, 2025 joint statement by Chairman Bost and Rep. Van Orden. In the same statement they said the plan was a partial claim program so veterans could stay in their homes. Congress passed it in July 2025, by voice vote in both chambers. Servicers have until November 28, 2026 to implement it. Which families were supposed to hold on for those sixteen months, and on what?”

heard: “VASP was never statutory. VA created it, so VA could end it.”
where: agency testimony · committee press releases · congressional replies
record_says: Congress did not write VASP. Congress did write the partial claim. Seven of the ten rules VA uses to decide who qualifies appear nowhere in that law.
authority: Congress enacted the Partial Claim Program at 38 U.S.C. § 3737 in the VA Home Loan Program Reform Act, Pub. L. 119-31, signed July 30 2025. Section 3737(a) sets three conditions for an eligible loan, including that the loan be “in default or at imminent risk of default.” VA’s own handbook, M26-4 Chapter 22, effective June 1 2026, lists ten qualifying criteria. Seven of the ten, § 22.02 a.2, a.4, a.5, a.6, a.7, a.8 and a.9, appear nowhere in the statute. Two of those seven were added after the public comment window closed: the 24-month modification lockout and the COVID partial claim bar.
say_back: “You are right that Congress did not create VASP. Congress did create the partial claim, in law, in July 2025. Congress wrote three conditions. VA’s handbook lists ten. Which statute authorizes the other seven?”
if_again: Ask, in writing to the committee of jurisdiction, for the statutory citation behind each of the seven handbook criteria.

heard: “The VA Home Loan Affordability Act caps seller concessions at six percent, the same as FHA.”
where: the sponsor’s one-pager · the committee rollout release · coverage repeating them
record_says: The bill text does not say that. It limits the seller fees actually paid by the veteran. A concession is money the seller puts toward the buyer’s costs, which is the opposite direction.
authority: H.R. 8532, the VA Home Loan Affordability Act. The sponsor’s one-pager says the bill would “cap seller concessions at 6% to match FHA standards for nonveterans.” The committee bill print, at SEC. 2(d)(3), adds a new paragraph to 38 U.S.C. 3710(b) reading that “the seller fees actually paid by the veteran do not exceed six percent of the outstanding balance of the loan.” Both documents are the sponsor’s own, published the same day. Nothing here says the bill is bad or that anyone misdescribed it on purpose; a one-pager is a summary, and the closing-cost cap in the same subsection is a real gain. Only the enacted text would govern.
say_back: “I want to check one thing against the bill itself. The one-pager says it caps seller concessions at six percent. The text at section 2(d)(3) says the seller fees actually paid by the veteran may not exceed six percent. A concession is what a seller puts toward my costs; that sentence is about what I pay. Which one does the bill do?”
if_again: Ask the sponsor’s office, in writing, to confirm which quantity paragraph (10) limits, and whether the one-pager will be corrected. The answer is checkable against the print rather than a matter of opinion.
